Many parts of cortex are wired in a similar way: neurons excite their close
neighbours and, through interneurons, inhibit cells a bit further away. This
"Mexican hat" arrangement is simple to write down, but what it does to
activity is not obvious at first sight. The short version is that such a
network has a favourite spatial scale. It amplifies activity patterns at one
particular wavelength and damps everything else, so almost any input comes
out striped. This is one of the standard explanations for periodic patterns
in cortex, such as orientation columns or the regular spacing of ocular
dominance bands (Swindale 1980; Ermentrout and Cowan 1979), and it is the
neural cousin of Turing's (1952) mechanism for patterns in chemistry and
development.

This page is in two parts. The first looks at the connection kernel alone and
asks which spatial frequency it favours. The second puts the kernel into a
network and lets you watch the stripes emerge. Everything runs in your
browser and updates while you move the sliders.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

exFont = ({size: getComputedStyle(document.body).fontSize, family: getComputedStyle(document.body).fontFamily, toString() { return this.size + " " + this.family; }})
exFg = () => getComputedStyle(document.body).color
mkCanvas = (W, H) => {
  const c = DOM.context2d(W, H);
  c.canvas.style.width = "100%"; c.canvas.style.maxWidth = W + "px"; c.canvas.style.height = "auto";
  return c;
}
axisBox = (c, x, y, w, h) => { c.strokeStyle = "#999"; c.lineWidth = 1; c.strokeRect(x, y, w, h); }
```

## Difference of Gaussians and its spectrum

Write the strength of the connection between two neurons as a function of
their distance. Excitation is a narrow Gaussian with width $\sigma_e$,
inhibition a wider one with width $\sigma_i$, and the kernel is the
difference of the two. Up close excitation wins and the kernel is positive;
further out the broader inhibition takes over and it becomes negative.

The useful trick is to look at this kernel in the Fourier domain. A
recurrent network applies the kernel to its activity over and over again,
and convolution with a kernel multiplies each spatial frequency of the
activity by the kernel's Fourier transform at that frequency. So the
transform tells you directly which frequencies get amplified on every pass
and which get suppressed. The Fourier transform of a Gaussian is again a
Gaussian, with a width inversely proportional to the original one. The
narrow excitatory Gaussian therefore covers a wide band of frequencies, the
broad inhibitory Gaussian only the low ones. Their difference is small at
frequency zero, where inhibition cancels excitation, rises to a peak, and
then falls off again once excitation runs out. That peak is the frequency
the network will favour.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof sigE = Inputs.range([0.1, 10], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Excitation width σₑ"})
viewof ampE = Inputs.range([0, 10], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Excitation strength"})
viewof sigI = Inputs.range([0.1, 10], {value: 2, step: 0.1, label: "Inhibition width σᵢ"})
viewof ampI = Inputs.range([0, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Inhibition strength"})

gauss = (x, s) => Math.exp(-0.5 * x * x / (s * s)) / (Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI) * s)
ghat = (f, s) => Math.exp(-2 * Math.PI * Math.PI * s * s * f * f)
xmax = 5 * Math.max(sigE, sigI)
space = Array.from({length: 401}, (_, i) => {
  const x = -xmax + 2 * xmax * i / 400;
  const e = ampE * gauss(x, sigE), inh = -ampI * gauss(x, sigI);
  return {x, Excitation: e, Inhibition: inh, "Difference of Gaussians": e + inh};
})
spectrum = Array.from({length: 401}, (_, i) => { const f = i / 400; return {f, k: Math.abs(ampE * ghat(f, sigE) - ampI * ghat(f, sigI))}; })
peak = spectrum.reduce((a, b) => (b.k > a.k ? b : a))

html`<div style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:1rem">
${Plot.plot({
  width: 370, height: 300, marginLeft: 40, marginBottom: 60, style: {fontSize: exFont.size, fontFamily: exFont.family},
  x: {label: "space", labelAnchor: "center", labelArrow: "none", labelOffset: 48},
  y: {label: null, ticks: 0},
  color: {legend: true, swatchSize: 18, style: {fontSize: exFont.size, fontFamily: exFont.family}, domain: ["Excitation", "Inhibition", "Difference of Gaussians"], range: ["#ff7f0e", "#1f77b4", "black"]},
  marks: [Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#999"}),
    ...["Excitation", "Inhibition", "Difference of Gaussians"].map(k => Plot.line(space, {x: "x", y: k, stroke: () => k, strokeWidth: 2}))]
})}
${Plot.plot({
  width: 370, height: 300, marginLeft: 55, marginBottom: 60, marginTop: 36, style: {fontSize: exFont.size, fontFamily: exFont.family},
  x: {label: "spatial frequency (cycles / unit)", labelAnchor: "center", labelArrow: "none", labelOffset: 48},
  y: {label: "|kernel spectrum|", labelArrow: "none", domain: [0, Math.max(0.05, ampE, ampI)]},
  marks: [Plot.line(spectrum, {x: "f", y: "k", stroke: "gray", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleX([peak.f], {stroke: "#ff7f0e", strokeDasharray: "4 4"}),
    Plot.text([peak], {x: "f", y: "k", text: d => `peak at f = ${d.f.toFixed(2)}`, dx: 8, dy: -8, textAnchor: "start"})]
})}
</div>`
```

The first plot shows the excitatory Gaussian in orange, the inhibitory one in
blue, drawn negative, and their difference in black. The second plot is the
magnitude of the kernel's Fourier transform, with the orange dashed line at
its peak. With the default settings the peak sits at about 0.15 cycles per
unit length, a wavelength of six to seven units, a few times the width of the
inhibitory surround.

A few things are worth trying before moving on. Make inhibition wider and
the peak moves to lower frequencies: the stripes the network will produce get
broader. Make excitation wider, closer to the inhibition width, and the peak
gets lower and broader, since the two Gaussians cancel over a larger range of
frequencies. Set the inhibition strength to zero and the peak moves to
frequency zero, meaning the network would simply amplify uniform activity
rather than any pattern. The Mexican hat shape, not just excitation, is what
makes stripes.

## Pattern formation in a recurrent network

Now wrap 256 neurons around a ring, so that there are no edges to worry
about, and connect each pair with a weight given by the kernel above. The
firing rates $r$ evolve according to

$$\tau \frac{dr}{dt} = -r + \left[\,W r + h\,\right]_+ .$$

Each neuron relaxes towards its total input with time constant $\tau$. The
input has two parts: the recurrent input $W r$ from the rest of the ring, and
an external input $h$ that is drawn at random once per neuron and then held
fixed. On top of that you can add noise that is redrawn at every time step.
The brackets denote rectification, so rates cannot go negative. The width
sliders set the two Gaussians of the kernel, in units of neurons along the
ring.

The gain slider is the one to watch. It scales the whole weight matrix so
that its largest eigenvalue equals the number you set. Because the kernel
depends only on distance, the eigenvectors of $W$ are sine waves around the
ring, one for each spatial frequency, and the eigenvalues are the kernel's
Fourier transform from the first part of the page. If the largest eigenvalue
is below 1, every pattern decays faster than the recurrence can feed it, and
the activity just reflects the random input. If it is above 1, the pattern
at the favoured frequency grows on each pass through the network until the
rectification stops it. That is the transition from a stable, input-driven
network to one that generates its own pattern.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof rnSigE = Inputs.range([1, 25], {value: 5, step: 0.5, label: "Excitation width"})
viewof rnSigI = Inputs.range([1, 50], {value: 12, step: 0.5, label: "Inhibition width"})
viewof rnGain = Inputs.range([0.2, 1.6], {value: 1.2, step: 0.02, label: "Gain (largest eigenvalue of W)"})
viewof rnNoise = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.1, step: 0.02, label: "Input noise"})
viewof rnPause = Inputs.toggle({label: "Pause"})
viewof rnReset = Inputs.button("Reset")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
rnN = 256
rnKernel = {
  const N = rnN, sE = rnSigE, sI = rnSigI;
  const g = (d, s) => Math.exp(-0.5 * d * d / (s * s)) / s;
  const k = new Float64Array(N);
  for (let d = 0; d < N; d++) { const dd = Math.min(d, N - d); k[d] = g(dd, sE) - g(dd, sI); }
  const ev = new Float64Array(N / 2 + 1);
  for (let m = 0; m <= N / 2; m++) { let s = 0; for (let d = 0; d < N; d++) s += k[d] * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * m * d / N); ev[m] = s; }
  let lmax = -Infinity, mmax = 0; for (let m = 0; m <= N / 2; m++) if (ev[m] > lmax) { lmax = ev[m]; mmax = m; }
  const scale = rnGain / lmax;
  return {N, k: k.map(x => x * scale), ev: ev.map(x => x * scale), mmax};
}
rnState = {
  rnReset;
  const N = rnN, dt = 0.1, tau = 1;
  const h = Float64Array.from({length: N}, () => 0.5 + 0.5 * Math.random());
  let r = new Float64Array(N).fill(0.5), t = 0;
  while (true) {
    if (!viewof rnPause.value) {
      const {k} = rnKernel; const noise = viewof rnNoise.value;
      for (let step = 0; step < 5; step++) {
        const rn = new Float64Array(N);
        for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) {
          let s = 0;
          for (let j = 0; j < N; j++) { const d = (i - j + N) % N; s += k[d] * r[j]; }
          rn[i] = r[i] + dt / tau * (-r[i] + Math.max(0, s + h[i] + noise * (Math.random() - 0.5) * 2));
        }
        r = rn; t += dt;
      }
    }
    yield {r, t};
  }
}
rnCanvas = mkCanvas(760, 400)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const {r, t} = rnState, {ev, mmax, N} = rnKernel, c = rnCanvas, fg = exFg();
  const W = 760, H = 400; c.clearRect(0, 0, W, H); c.font = exFont;
  const aP = {x0: 90, y0: 12, w: W - 110, h: 170};
  const rmax = Math.max(1e-6, ...r);
  axisBox(c, aP.x0, aP.y0, aP.w, aP.h);
  c.fillStyle = "#1f77b4";
  for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) { const bh = aP.h * r[i] / rmax; c.fillRect(aP.x0 + aP.w * i / N, aP.y0 + aP.h - bh, aP.w / N, bh); }
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "right"; c.fillText("activity", aP.x0 - 8, aP.y0 + aP.h / 2 + 5);
  c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText(`position on the ring · t = ${t.toFixed(0)} τ`, aP.x0 + aP.w / 2, aP.y0 + aP.h + 22);
  const sP = {x0: 90, y0: 240, w: W - 110, h: 110};
  const M = 40, emax = Math.max(1.6, ...ev), emin = Math.min(-0.5, ...ev);
  const sy = v => sP.y0 + sP.h * (1 - (v - emin) / (emax - emin));
  axisBox(c, sP.x0, sP.y0, sP.w, sP.h);
  c.setLineDash([4, 4]); c.strokeStyle = "red"; c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(sP.x0, sy(1)); c.lineTo(sP.x0 + sP.w, sy(1)); c.stroke(); c.setLineDash([]);
  c.strokeStyle = "#888"; c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(sP.x0, sy(0)); c.lineTo(sP.x0 + sP.w, sy(0)); c.stroke();
  for (let m = 0; m <= M; m++) { c.fillStyle = m === mmax ? "#ff7f0e" : "gray"; c.beginPath(); c.arc(sP.x0 + sP.w * m / M, sy(ev[m]), 4, 0, 2 * Math.PI); c.fill(); }
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "right"; c.fillText("eigenvalue", sP.x0 - 8, sP.y0 + sP.h / 2 + 5); c.fillText("1", sP.x0 - 8, sy(1) + 5); c.fillText("0", sP.x0 - 8, sy(0) + 5);
  c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText(`spatial frequency (waves around the ring) · amplified most: ${mmax}`, sP.x0 + sP.w / 2, sP.y0 + sP.h + 22);
  c.fillText("0", sP.x0, sP.y0 + sP.h + 42); c.fillText(M, sP.x0 + sP.w, sP.y0 + sP.h + 42);
  return c.canvas;
}
```

## Reading the figure

The upper panel shows the activity of every neuron as a bar, laid out by
position on the ring, with the clock in units of $\tau$ underneath. The
lower panel shows the eigenvalues of $W$, one grey dot for each spatial
frequency, counted in whole waves around the ring. This is the same curve as
the kernel spectrum in the first part of the page, just sampled at the
frequencies that fit on the ring and scaled by the gain. The orange dot is
the largest eigenvalue, and the red dashed line marks the value 1, the
boundary between decay and growth.

With the default settings the gain is 1.2 and the orange dot sits above the
line. After a moment the activity organises into a regular set of bumps, and
if you count them you will find the number next to the orange dot. The
random input is still there, which is why the bumps are not all the same
height, but the spacing is set entirely by the kernel.

## Things to try

Pull the gain below 1 and press Reset. The bumps fade and what is left is a
noisy copy of the random input: the network is now a filter that smooths its
input a little, nothing more. Push the gain back above 1 and the pattern
grows back, from whatever small ripples in the input happen to match the
favoured frequency. Near the threshold the growth is slow and you can watch
it happen.

Make the inhibition wider. The orange dot moves left, to a lower frequency,
and after a Reset the bumps are fewer and broader. Make excitation wider
instead and the bumps get broader too, but the peak of the spectrum also
gets flatter, so neighbouring frequencies compete and the pattern takes
longer to settle.

Turn the noise up. The pattern survives surprisingly well, because the
network amplifies only the component of the noise at its favourite frequency
and ignores the rest. This is the sense in which a recurrent network with a
Mexican hat kernel imposes its own structure on whatever it is given, and
why the same mechanism has been proposed for so many different periodic
patterns in the brain.

This page is based on the pattern-formation exercise in Dayan and Abbott
(2001, chapter 7). The ring network with a distance-dependent kernel is the
setting of Amari's (1977) analysis of neural fields, and the same
architecture, with the ring standing for preferred orientation rather than
position, is the ring model of orientation tuning of Ben-Yishai et al.
(1995).
